title: Suspiro de Limena
subtitle: Peruvian caramel custard topped with port meringue
excerpt: Suspiro de limena is a two-part Peruvian dessert: a thick, sweet caramel custard made from condensed and evaporated milk, topped with a glossy port-wine Italian meringue. It is chilled before serving and dusted with ground cinnamon. The contrast between the dense, sweet base and the airy meringue is what makes it distinctive.
sourceNotes: Suspiro de limena means sigh of a Lima woman, a name given to the dessert by the Peruvian poet Jose Galvez in tribute to his wife, who created the recipe. It has been a fixture on Lima restaurant menus since the early twentieth century and is considered one of the great desserts of Peruvian cuisine.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The custard base can be made a day ahead. Add the meringue no more than 2 hours before serving.

content.text: This recipe serves 6 and takes about 50 minutes of active cooking plus 2 hours of chilling time. The base is a thick caramel custard made by cooking condensed milk, 400ml evaporated milk and egg yolks together over low heat, stirred constantly until the mixture pulls away from the sides of the pan. The topping is an Italian meringue made with port wine syrup poured over whipped egg whites.

Italian meringue requires a sugar thermometer. The port syrup must reach 118C before being poured onto the egg whites, or the meringue will not hold. Keep the mixer running as you pour the syrup in a thin, steady stream. Do not rush this step. The custard base must be fully cooled and set before the meringue goes on, or the two layers will mix together.

Combine the condensed milk and 400ml evaporated milk in a heavy-based saucepan. Cook over medium-low heat, stirring constantly with a wooden spoon or spatula, for 20 to 25 minutes. The mixture will darken slightly and thicken until it pulls away from the sides of the pan.

Remove from the heat. Whisk the 4 egg yolks in a bowl. Add a ladleful of the hot milk mixture to the yolks slowly, whisking constantly. This tempers the yolks so they do not scramble. Pour the yolk mixture back into the saucepan and stir over low heat for 3 more minutes.
Stir in 1 tsp vanilla extract. Pour the custard into 6 individual serving glasses or one large dish. Leave to cool to room temperature, then refrigerate for at least 2 hours until set.

When the custard is set and cold, make the Italian meringue. Combine 120g caster sugar and 120ml port wine in a small saucepan. Bring to the boil and cook without stirring until the syrup reaches 118C on a sugar thermometer.
While the syrup cooks, whisk the 4 egg whites in a clean bowl with an electric mixer until they hold soft peaks.

With the mixer running on medium-high speed, pour the hot port syrup down the side of the bowl in a thin, steady stream. Do not pour onto the beaters. Once all the syrup is in, increase to high speed and whisk for 5 to 7 minutes until the meringue is thick, glossy and has cooled to room temperature.
Spoon or pipe the meringue over the cold custard. Dust generously with ground cinnamon. Serve straight away or keep refrigerated for up to 2 hours before serving.

attrs.symptom: Custard base is lumpy or scrambled
attrs.cause: The egg yolks were added to the hot milk mixture too quickly
attrs.fix: Always temper the yolks by adding the hot milk to them gradually while whisking before combining with the full pan. Keep the heat low throughout.

attrs.symptom: Meringue is flat and runny rather than glossy and stiff
attrs.cause: The port syrup was not hot enough when poured in, or the egg whites were over-beaten before the syrup was added
attrs.fix: Use a sugar thermometer and wait until the syrup reaches exactly 118C. Stop beating the egg whites at soft peaks, not stiff, before the syrup goes in.

attrs.cause: The custard was not cold enough before the meringue was added
attrs.fix: Chill the custard for the full 2 hours until it is completely set and cold before topping with the meringue.

content.text: Suspiro de limena is one of the signature desserts of Lima and appears on restaurant menus throughout Peru. It is a special-occasion dish in home kitchens, made when there is time and reason to put in the effort. The name and the story behind it have made it famous well beyond Peru's borders.
